steps.title: Altitude and lava
steps.body: Etna's vineyards climb its slopes from about 400 to over 1,000 m, mostly on the north, east and south sides. Altitude gives cool nights and late harvests into October. Soils are volcanic sand, ash and lava, poor and well-drained. Phylloxera can't survive easily, so many old vines are ungrafted bush vines, alberello, on terraces.

steps.title: Contrade
steps.body: Etna's vineyards are divided into contrade, local districts often defined by different lava flows. Since 2011, 133 contrade can appear on labels, like Burgundy's crus. Etna DOC, one of Italy's first, from 1968, covers red, white, rosé and sparkling. Etna Rosso must be at least 80% Nerello Mascalese; Etna Bianco at least 60% Carricante.

options: Local districts often defined by lava flows
steps.explanation: Each contrada has its own soil and character.

steps.title: The revival
steps.body: Etna's modern revival began around 2000, when producers like Frank Cornelissen, Andrea Franchetti and Marc de Grazia arrived, and local families like Benanti invested. Its reds, pale and perfumed, are often compared with Burgundy and Barolo. Its whites, from Carricante, are mineral and long-lived.

steps.explanation: Etna's vineyards are steep and poor, not flat and fertile.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Etna's vineyards climb to over 1,000 m on volcanic soils
Its revival since 2000 made Nerello and Carricante famous
